title: Word origins
notice: Origins are checked against Wiktionary etymologies; many words passed through other languages on the way to English.

items.name: robot
items.blurb: “robot” comes from Czech. From robota, "forced labour"; first used in Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R.

items.name: shampoo
items.blurb: “shampoo” comes from Hindi. From a word meaning "to press" or "massage".

items.name: pyjamas
items.blurb: “pyjamas” comes from Hindi and Urdu. From words meaning "leg garment".

items.name: bungalow
items.blurb: “bungalow” comes from Hindi. Originally "a house in the Bengal style".

items.name: jungle
items.blurb: “jungle” comes from Hindi. From a word for wild, uncultivated land.

items.name: kindergarten
items.blurb: “kindergarten” comes from German. "Children's garden".

items.name: hamburger

items.name: emoji

items.name: tycoon

items.name: kayak

questions.prompt: The word "emoji" comes from the English word "emotion".
questions.explain: It is Japanese: e ("picture") plus moji ("character"). The likeness is a coincidence.

questions.prompt: "Posh" stands for "Port Out, Starboard Home".
questions.explain: That is a later invented explanation; no evidence supports it.

questions.prompt: "Golf" stands for "Gentlemen Only, Ladies Forbidden".
questions.explain: A modern joke. The word goes back to Scots in the 1400s.

questions.prompt: "SOS" stands for "Save Our Souls".
questions.explain: SOS was chosen because its Morse code (three dots, three dashes, three dots) is easy to send and recognise.

questions.prompt: "Goodbye" is a shortened form of "God be with you".
questions.explain: The phrase was squeezed down over the 1500s and 1600s.

questions.prompt: "Muscle" comes from a Latin word meaning "little mouse".
questions.explain: Latin musculus: a flexing muscle was thought to look like a mouse moving under the skin.

questions.prompt: "Disaster" literally means "bad star".
questions.explain: From Italian disastro: an ill-starred event, from the idea that stars rule our fate.

questions.prompt: "Quarantine" comes from an Italian phrase for "forty days".
questions.explain: Ships arriving in Venice during plagues had to wait forty days before landing.

questions.prompt: "Malaria" comes from Italian words for "bad air".
questions.explain: People once blamed the disease on foul air from swamps.

questions.prompt: "Clue" comes from "clew", a ball of thread.
questions.explain: In the Greek myth, Theseus used a ball of thread to find his way out of the Labyrinth.

questions.prompt: The word "robot" was first used in a play.
questions.explain: Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. introduced it.

questions.prompt: John Milton coined the word "pandemonium".
questions.explain: In Paradise Lost (1667) it is the capital of Hell: "all the demons".

questions.prompt: "Serendipity" was coined by the writer Horace Walpole.
questions.explain: He made it up in 1754, from a fairy tale called The Three Princes of Serendip.

questions.prompt: Lewis Carroll coined the word "chortle".
questions.explain: It first appeared in Through the Looking-Glass (1871), blending "chuckle" and "snort".

questions.prompt: Thomas More coined the word "utopia".
questions.explain: His 1516 book Utopia named an ideal island; the Greek means "no place".

questions.prompt: "Nice" once meant "foolish" or "ignorant".
questions.explain: It comes from Latin nescius, "not knowing", and changed meaning over centuries.

questions.prompt: "Quiz" was invented by a Dublin theatre owner who bet he could get a nonsense word into the language overnight.
questions.explain: The story is a legend; the word was already in use before the supposed bet.

questions.prompt: "Hippopotamus" comes from Greek words meaning "river horse".
questions.explain: Hippos means horse and potamos means river.

questions.prompt: "Dinosaur" means "terrible lizard".
questions.explain: Richard Owen coined it in 1842 from Greek deinos ("terrible") and sauros ("lizard").

questions.prompt: "Astronaut" means "star sailor".
questions.explain: From Greek astron ("star") and nautes ("sailor").

questions.prompt: Which day of the week is named after the Norse god of thunder, Thor?
questions.explain: Thursday is "Thor's day".

questions.prompt: Which day of the week is named after the god Woden (Odin)?
questions.explain: Wednesday is "Woden's day".

questions.prompt: Which day of the week is named after the Roman god Saturn?
questions.explain: Saturday is "Saturn's day".

questions.prompt: Which month is named after Janus, the two-faced Roman god of doorways?
questions.explain: Janus looks both back to the old year and forward to the new.

questions.prompt: Which month is named after Julius Caesar?
questions.explain: The Romans renamed the month Quintilis in his honour.

questions.prompt: Which month is named after the emperor Augustus?
questions.explain: The month Sextilis was renamed in his honour.

questions.prompt: October comes from the Latin word for which number?
questions.explain: October was the eighth month of the early Roman calendar, which began in March.

questions.prompt: The word "panic" comes from which Greek god?
questions.explain: Pan was believed to cause sudden fear in lonely places.

questions.prompt: The word "cereal" comes from which Roman goddess?
questions.explain: Ceres was the goddess of grain and farming.
